topic_title: The Strange Pull of Delivery Tracking

sources.title: Worry and information-seeking during uncertain waiting periods (as reported in "When Waiting Feels Unbearable, We Chase Clues")
sources.authors_or_organization: Howell, J.L., Sweeny, K. (original study); Saul McLeod, PhD / Simply Psychology (secondary report)
sources.journal_or_venue: Emotion, Vol. 25(7), pp. 1774-1783 (American Psychological Association); summarized by Simply Psychology (2025-10-02, updated 2025-11-12)
sources.fetched_extraction: Longitudinal research tracking three groups through uncertain waiting periods over weeks and months: U.S. voters in the run-up to the 2020 election, law school graduates awaiting California bar exam results, and academic job seekers awaiting hiring decisions. Key finding: 'the more people worried, the more they chased information' -- worry spikes predicted corresponding increases in news-checking and update-seeking behavior. This contradicts the common assumption that anxiety leads people to avoid information; instead, participants showed strong information-seeking during peak worry. The proposed psychological mechanism is that seeking information creates a 'fragile sense of control' during an otherwise uncontrollable situation, though the relief is temporary and can perpetuate anxiety cycles (checking again soon after). NOTE: this extraction is based on a secondary summary (Simply Psychology) of the original journal article, not a direct fetch of the Emotion journal article itself.

sources.title: Joint contributions of metacognition and self-beliefs to uncertainty-guided checking behavior
sources.authors_or_organization: Baptista, Axel; Maheu, Maxime; Mallet, Luc; N'Diaye, Karim
sources.fetched_extraction: A behavioral experiment with 28 healthy participants (ages 19-29, mean age 23.6). Participants completed four tasks over 1.5 hours: a calibration phase, a checking task (judging the direction of random dot motion stimuli they could replay an unlimited number of times before deciding, at calibrated difficulty levels), an implicit metacognition task, an explicit metacognition task, and questionnaires assessing cognitive mistrust and obsessive-compulsive symptoms. Key findings: participants increased their checking frequency for more difficult (more uncertain) stimuli (b=0.90, P<2x10^-16), directly demonstrating that uncertainty drives checking behavior. Explicit metacognition (conscious awareness of one's own uncertainty) predicted this uncertainty-regulated checking (b=0.08, P=0.028), while implicit metacognition did not (b=-0.05, P=0.210); the two metacognition measures were statistically independent of each other across participants (r=0.04, P=0.853). Self-reported cognitive mistrust significantly reduced the effect of stimulus difficulty on checking behavior (b=-0.09, P=0.039), while self-reported obsessive-compulsive symptoms increased it (b=0.10, P=0.019).
